sourceCourseTitle: Ai Governance Compliance Responsible Ai Leader / Audit and Incident Response

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to design and operate an enterprise AI system registry as a single source of truth 2) Which metadata fields enable auditability, risk management, and fast incident response 3) How to integrate the registry with SDLC/MLOps to keep entries current and enforce governance

blocks.title: Red Teaming AI: OWASP LLM Top 10
blocks.label: Course Video

body.en:
An AI system registry is a centralized inventory of all AI/ML systems, models, datasets, and related services across the organization. It provides traceability from business purpose to technical artifacts and operational controls, enabling compliance, risk assessment, and rapid incident handling.

Scope and purpose: The registry covers models (including LLMs and fine-tunes), datasets, pipelines, prompts/agents, evaluation suites, deployments, and downstream integrations that act on AI outputs. It links to owners, approvers, and on-call contacts to support accountability.

Regulatory alignment: A registry supports obligations in GDPR (Records of Processing Activities when personal data is processed), the EU AI Act (risk classification, technical documentation, post-market monitoring), sector rules (e.g., model governance in finance/health), and frameworks like NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 AI management systems.

Minimum critical fields: Business purpose and allowed use; system owner and accountable executive; risk classification and justification; data categories (PII, sensitive attributes, special categories); training and evaluation datasets with lineage; model provenance and version/commit hash; deployment environments and endpoints; access controls and consumer apps; human-in-the-loop/override; pre-deployment reviews (privacy impact/DPIA, algorithmic impact assessments); evaluation results (performance, robustness, bias/fairness); red-teaming outcomes; monitoring metrics and alert thresholds; incident runbook, rollback/kill-switch location; vendor dependencies and licenses; change history and approvals.

Lifecycle and automation: Create entries at proposal stage, update at each material change, and retire with archival of artifacts and logs. Enforce completeness via CI/CD gates (e.g., block deployment if mandatory fields or risk reviews are missing). Auto-populate fields from MLOps (model registries, feature stores), IaC (environments, endpoints), and security tooling (SBOM/MBOM, vulnerability scans). Tag releases and pin versions for reproducibility.

Incident response linkage: The registry must make it easy to find on-call contacts, affected services, last safe version, and rollback steps. It should store monitoring metrics, evaluation baselines, and known failure modes to accelerate triage. Access should be searchable and permissioned, with audit logs of who changed what and when.

• Single source of truth: A centralized, authoritative inventory that links business purpose to technical and risk artifacts
• Risk-critical metadata: Owner/on-call, data categories, evaluations, red-team results, versioning, and kill-switch details enable fast audits and incident response
• Lifecycle integration: CI/CD and MLOps automation keep entries current and enforce governance before deployment

question.en: A team is about to deploy a fine-tuned LLM behind an internal API. Which registry elements are most essential to ensure effective incident response if outputs become harmful?

text.en: Marketing description and user satisfaction survey links
On-call contacts, kill-switch/rollback plan, model version/commit hash, and monitoring thresholds
Office location of the team and weekly standup notes
Only the base model name used for fine-tuning

explanation.en: Incident response relies on accountable contacts, how to disable/rollback safely, exact versioning to reproduce, and monitoring to detect issues quickly.

question.en: For an AI system potentially in scope of the EU AI Act, what should the registry capture to support compliance?

text.en: Only a link to a press release announcing the system
A list of team members and their favorite tools
Risk classification with justification, technical documentation, evaluation/red-team evidence, post-market monitoring plan, and conformity artifacts
A screenshot of the UI

explanation.en: The EU AI Act expects documented risk classification, technical and testing evidence, and post-market monitoring to be maintained and auditable.

question.en: How can you keep the registry accurate as models and endpoints change frequently?

text.en: Integrate registry updates into CI/CD, auto-ingest from MLOps/IaC, and block deploys if mandatory fields are missing
Rely on quarterly manual spreadsheets only
Allow teams to update when convenient with no checks
Create a registry entry only at project kickoff and never update it

explanation.en: Automation via CI/CD and integrations keeps data current and enforceable; deploy gates prevent drift and shadow AI.

body.en:
• Maintain a centralized registry linking business purpose, risk, and technical artifacts
• Capture risk-critical metadata (owners, data categories, evaluations, red-team results, versions, kill switch)
• Automate updates via CI/CD/MLOps and use deploy gates to enforce completeness and approvals
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to build and operate an AI system registry that enables compliance, auditability, and fast incident response.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to assess and onboard external AI vendors and models 2) Which contractual, security, and compliance controls reduce third-party and model risk 3) How to monitor vendors/models and coordinate incident response and continuity

Vendor and model risk management ensures third-party AI services and external models meet organizational, security, and regulatory requirements.

Due diligence: Evaluate use case risk, data sensitivity, and impact. Review vendor security posture (SOC 2 Type II, ISO/IEC 27001), AI governance maturity (alignment to NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001), privacy practices (DPA, data residency, cross-border transfers), and incident response processes (RACI, notification SLAs). Verify safe-by-design practices: red-teaming, safety filters, content moderation, prompt injection defenses, and abuse monitoring.

Data handling and IP: Confirm how prompts/outputs are stored, encrypted, and retained; whether data is used to train or fine-tune provider models; availability of zero-retention or customer-controlled encryption; and terms around model/IP licensing and attribution. Require restrictions on training with customer data unless explicitly allowed.

Model-specific controls: Demand model cards or equivalent documentation (intended use, limitations, evaluation metrics, bias/fairness evidence), version pinning, and change notifications. Validate robustness to known threats (prompt injection, data exfiltration, jailbreaks), and require red-team reports or your own validation before production. Track dependencies (datasets, open-source components) and provenance/attestations (signed artifacts, Model/AI BOM where available).

Contracts and SLAs: Include uptime/performance SLAs, rate limits, data protection terms, security requirements, audit/assessment rights, breach notification timelines, and required support for incident investigations. Define kill-switch/rollback options, termination assistance, and data deletion/return.

Ongoing monitoring: Continuously evaluate model quality, safety, latency, and cost. Watch for silent model updates; enforce canary testing and phased rollouts. Manage concentration risk with fallback providers and routing controls. Log vendor issues in your registry and tie to playbooks for coordinated incident response.

blocks.label: Recommended Viewing

body.en:
• Third-party due diligence: Assess security, privacy, governance maturity, and safety practices before onboarding
• Model governance with vendors: Require documentation, evaluations, version pinning, and change notifications
• Resilience and monitoring: SLAs, outage playbooks, fallback providers, and continuous evaluation mitigate operational and safety risk

question.en: A startup offers a high-performing text model but retains prompts for training. You plan to process regulated personal data. What is the minimum contractual control to proceed safely?

text.en: Ask the vendor to verbally confirm good intentions
Rely on the vendor's marketing website for assurances
Execute a DPA prohibiting training on your data, require encryption and strict retention/deletion, and enable a zero-retention mode
Proceed without a contract but throttle requests

explanation.en: A robust DPA with explicit no-training, encryption, and retention controls is required for regulated data; marketing claims are insufficient.

question.en: Your application broke after the vendor silently switched the default model version. Which control would have prevented the disruption?

text.en: Version pinning with change approval and canary testing before rollout
Increasing the API timeout by 5 seconds
Using a different programming language
Sending more traffic to the vendor to stabilize results

explanation.en: Pinning to a specific version and requiring staged rollout prevents untested upgrades from reaching production.

question.en: A third-party LLM API suffers a regional outage. What is the most effective resilience strategy?

text.en: Retry indefinitely on the same endpoint
Implement multi-vendor fallback with health checks, routing/circuit breakers, and graceful degradation
Pause all AI features until the quarterly review
Send alerts but take no technical action

explanation.en: Redundancy across providers and automated routing/circuit breakers maintain service and reduce incident impact.

body.en:
• Perform structured due diligence and require strong DPAs, SLAs, and safety evidence before onboarding
• Enforce model documentation, evaluations, and version pinning with change notifications
• Monitor continuously and build resilience with fallbacks, canaries, and incident coordination with vendors
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now evaluate and manage vendor/model risk and coordinate effective incident response.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) Identify, triage, and classify AI incidents and near-misses 2) Execute compliant reporting to regulators, customers, and internal stakeholders 3) Design an effective post-market monitoring program with metrics, tooling, and CAPA to prevent recurrence

An AI incident is an event where an AI system causes or could reasonably cause harm (e.g., safety, financial, privacy, security, fairness, rights). Near-misses warrant learning as much as realized harms.

Establish an incident taxonomy and severity levels (e.g., SEV-1 to SEV-3) with SLAs, an incident commander, and a cross‑functional team (AI/ML, product, legal, privacy, security, compliance, comms). Preserve evidence with immutable logs, versioned models/data, and chain of custody; consider legal privilege for investigations.

Reporting obligations span internal alerts, customer notifications per contract, and regulatory rules (e.g., personal data breaches under GDPR may require notifying authorities within 72 hours; sectoral/product rules can impose additional timelines). High‑risk AI use cases should have post‑market monitoring (PMM): continuous tracking of performance, robustness, safety, and fairness using metrics such as drift, false positives/negatives, hallucination/toxicity/refusal rates, disparity ratios, and human override rates; include red teaming, canary releases, and complaint/feedback channels.

Perform root‑cause analysis (5 Whys, Fishbone) and implement CAPA—corrective fixes (rollbacks, rule/guardrail updates, access controls) and preventive measures (data curation, re‑training, process/policy updates, additional tests). Integrate with existing security incident response and SOC processes, run tabletop exercises, and document lessons learned.

Align with frameworks like NIST AI RMF (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) and ISO/IEC 23894 (risk management) and operationalize within an AI management system (e.g., ISO/IEC 42001).

• Incident taxonomy and severity: Define what counts as an AI incident/near-miss and how to classify impact and urgency.
• Reporting workflows and timelines: Clear triggers, owners, approvals, and channels for internal, customer, and regulatory notifications.
• Post-market monitoring and CAPA: Continuous metrics, feedback loops, root-cause analysis, and corrective/preventive actions to reduce recurrence.

question.en: A deployed LLM starts producing discriminatory loan recommendations for a protected group. What is the best immediate action?

text.en: Wait 24 hours to collect more examples before acting
Activate the incident response playbook: contain exposure (e.g., rollback/disable pathway), preserve logs/artifacts, and escalate to the incident commander
Publish a public statement before internal triage is complete
Delete all logs to reduce legal exposure

explanation.en: Prompt containment, evidence preservation, and structured escalation minimize harm and enable compliant reporting and remediation.

question.en: A model update leads to occasional leakage of personal data in outputs. Which external reporting timeline is most relevant to consider first?

text.en: No external reporting is ever required for model errors
Only the annual transparency report
Data protection breach notification timelines (e.g., GDPR’s 72-hour rule where applicable)
Wait until the next product release cycle

explanation.en: Personal data exposure may trigger data protection breach notifications (e.g., GDPR's 72-hour timeline) in addition to any sectoral/product obligations.

question.en: Which element is most critical to include in a post-market monitoring plan for a high-risk AI system?

text.en: Defined risk metrics, thresholds, monitoring coverage, and feedback/complaint intake with clear owners
Only a high-level statement that the model is accurate
A marketing plan to promote AI features
A single manual test at launch

explanation.en: Effective PMM requires measurable metrics, thresholds, coverage targets, and clear ownership to detect and act on emerging risks.

body.en:
• Define incidents, severities, roles, and SLAs; run playbooks and preserve evidence.
• Meet internal, customer, and regulatory reporting duties; align with privacy and sector rules.
• Implement PMM with metrics, feedback loops, RCA, and CAPA to continuously reduce risk.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to report AI incidents and operate a post-market monitoring program that detects, contains, and prevents harms.

blocks.title: AI Provider, Deployer & Other Roles According to ISO 42001
blocks.label: Tutorial

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) Build concise, decision-ready executive dashboards and board packs 2) Select KPIs/KRIs and thresholds aligned to risk appetite and regulation 3) Communicate incidents, assurance results, and remediation status with clear ownership and timelines

Executive reporting translates complex AI risk and performance into decisions. A board pack should include: an AI system inventory and risk classification; a risk heat map and top risks; incident summaries and trends (e.g., SEV-1 rate, MTTD/MTTR, root causes); compliance status against applicable laws (e.g., AI use classification, privacy, sector regulations); assurance results (internal audit, external attestations, red-teaming) and control effectiveness; key KPIs/KRIs (performance vs targets, fairness disparity ratios, toxicity/hallucination rates, robustness/adversarial test coverage, monitoring coverage, model change frequency, human oversight efficacy); third‑party/foundation model risk; exceptions and waivers; resourcing, training, and budget; and forward‑looking approvals/decisions needed.

Use clear thresholds, trendlines, and traffic‑light status. Define decision rights and escalation criteria (what triggers ad‑hoc board notification vs quarterly cadence) and map RACI across management, risk, and audit committees.

Align with NIST AI RMF governance and AI management systems (e.g., ISO/IEC 42001) so board oversight matches stated risk appetite and strategy. Keep narrative plain‑language, blameless but accountable, and include a one‑page executive summary with appendices for detail.

• Board pack structure: Inventory, risk heat map, incidents/trends, compliance and assurance, decisions required, and appendices.
• KPIs/KRIs and thresholds: Metrics that reflect harm, fairness, robustness, performance, and control effectiveness with clear targets.
• Escalation and decision rights: Materiality criteria, RACI, and committee roles to act on incidents and approvals.

question.en: Which set of metrics best signals AI risk trends for an executive dashboard?

text.en: Total lines of model code and number of features
SEV-1 incident rate, MTTD/MTTR, fairness disparity ratios, toxicity/hallucination rates, and model change frequency
Daily active users only
Marketing campaign impressions

explanation.en: These KRIs/KPIs directly reflect harm, timeliness of detection/response, bias/safety issues, and operational volatility.

question.en: A material AI incident meets your escalation threshold two weeks before the next board meeting. What should you do?

text.en: Wait for the scheduled meeting to avoid alarming the board
Circulate only a technical postmortem to engineers
Provide an ad-hoc update to the chair/committee per the escalation protocol, with impact, containment, and next steps
Take no action until media coverage appears

explanation.en: Material incidents require timely off-cycle notification with clear facts, actions, and decisions needed.

question.en: What belongs in the board pack’s approvals section for high-risk AI?

text.en: Proposed risk appetite updates and go-live decisions for high-risk models with owners, controls, and timelines
Detailed training hyperparameters for every experiment
Only a celebratory note on AI innovation
A list of office snacks for the data science team

explanation.en: Boards should decide on risk appetite and high-risk approvals, ensuring controls and accountability are in place before launch.

body.en:
• Board packs should be decision-oriented: concise summaries, clear KRIs/KPIs, and explicit asks.
• Use thresholds, trends, and RACI to drive timely escalation and accountability.
• Link oversight to recognized frameworks and your AI management system to evidence control effectiveness.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now craft executive and board-ready AI risk reports that enable effective oversight and timely decisions.
